name: Kinetin

card.summary: A plant-hormone-type molecule (N6-furfuryladenine) used in cosmeceutical creams that aim to smooth fine lines, improve texture and calm sensitive skin.
card.note: Cosmetic ingredient; research on skin is limited to small trials and reviews.

quick.overview:
Kinetin is a synthetic cytokinin, a class of plant hormones that promote cell division, first isolated in 1955 from degraded DNA. In skincare it is sold as a gentle anti-ageing ingredient meant to even skin tone, reduce fine lines and improve barrier function, often in lotions at about 0.1%.

Small human trials, including a randomised split-face study with niacinamide in Asian participants and an open-label rosacea study, examined effects on ageing signs and rosacea. A dermatology review from 2000 noted that its mechanism in human skin was not established at that time.
quick.how: It is applied as a leave-on lotion or cream, with the rosacea study using twice-daily application of a 0.1% lotion, and is often found alongside other cosmeceutical ingredients such as niacinamide. Cosmetic users commonly expect gradual changes over weeks.
quick.risks: Kinetin lotion was studied in people with rosacea, who often have very sensitive skin, partly because it was thought to support barrier function. As with any topical, irritation or allergy is possible. It is sold as a cosmetic rather than a drug.

lead: Kinetin, chemically 6-furfurylaminopurine, is a synthetic cytokinin that promotes cell division in plants. It was isolated by Carlos Miller and Folke Skoog from autoclaved herring sperm DNA and named for its ability to induce cell division in tissue culture; later work suggested it is formed naturally in DNA from furfural, an oxidative damage product [1][2].

In skincare, it is positioned as an anti-photoageing ingredient that supports skin barrier function. A 2000 dermatology review used kinetin as an example of how to assess a new cosmeceutical, asking whether it penetrates the skin, whether a plausible mechanism exists and whether controlled trials are published, and noted that its mechanism in human skin was unknown at that point [3].
Randomised and open-label studies since then have looked at kinetin with niacinamide for ageing signs and at kinetin 0.1% lotion for rosacea [4][5].

chain: Supports barrier function and antioxidant defence
angle.text: Kinetin creams are used to soften the look of fine lines and uneven texture and to calm reactive skin. Small trials, one with niacinamide, have examined these signs.

paras: In plant science kinetin is used in tissue culture to induce callus and shoots [1][6]. In cosmetics it is used in anti-ageing lotions that claim to improve photodamaged skin and barrier function [3][4].
A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled split-face trial studied topical kinetin with niacinamide for ageing signs in Asian participants [4].

An open-label study of twice-daily kinetin 0.1% lotion in people with rosacea examined tolerance and efficacy for improving the signs and symptoms of the condition; the investigators suggested kinetin may help restore barrier function [5].

The 2000 review raised the question of whether topical nucleotides can penetrate photodamaged skin and said the mechanism of kinetin in human skin was not established, noting that antioxidant action would not by itself explain any reversal of photoageing [3]. Later reviews describe kinetin as a multi-active molecule that affects differentiation of human cells [6].
Kinetin was isolated in 1955 and for a long time was thought to be an artefact of DNA degradation; since 1996 researchers have reported it occurs naturally in the DNA of many organisms [1][2].

timeline.event: Miller and Skoog isolate kinetin from autoclaved herring sperm DNA [1].
Dermatologic Clinics review uses kinetin as an example for evaluating cosmeceuticals [3].
Trials of kinetin for rosacea and with niacinamide for ageing signs are published [4][5].
